primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: An anatomically narrow anterior chamber angle can abruptly close when the peripheral iris obstructs the trabecular meshwork, rapidly increasing intraocular pressure.
vignette: A 67-year-old woman develops sudden severe unilateral eye pain, headache, nausea, blurred vision, and colored halos around lights. Examination shows conjunctival injection, a cloudy cornea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
distractors: Open-angle glaucoma
Anterior uveitis
Central retinal artery occlusion
Optic neuritis
distractor_notes: Open-angle glaucoma is usually chronic and painless without an acutely fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Anterior uveitis commonly causes photophobia and a constricted or irregular pupil rather than marked acute angle closure.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless monocular vision loss, not a painful red eye with halos.
Optic neuritis causes painful eye movement and visual loss but not a cloudy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, or acute high-pressure phenotype.
key_expl: Acute angle closure causes sudden obstruction of aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork, producing rapid intraocular-pressure elevation with severe pain, halos, nausea, corneal edema, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
objective: Recognize acute angle-closure glaucoma from its characteristic painful red-eye and high-pressure clinical syndrome.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Granulomatous inflammation of medium and large arteries, often cranial branches of the carotid, causes luminal narrowing and ischemic complications including jaw claudication and visual loss.
vignette: A 74-year-old woman develops a new unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, fatigue, and jaw pain while chewing. ESR and CRP are markedly elevated, and she reports a brief episode of monocular visual loss.
distractors: Trigeminal neuralgia
Migraine with aura
Polyarteritis nodosa
Takayasu arteritis
distractor_notes: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric facial pain and does not explain elevated inflammatory markers, jaw claudication, and visual ischemia.
Migraine can cause visual aura but not the classic older-age inflammatory vasculitic syndrome with jaw claudication.
Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that typically spares the pulmonary circulation and does not characteristically target temporal arteries.
Takayasu arteritis affects large vessels mainly in younger women and presents with pulse/BP discrepancies rather than this cranial syndrome.
key_expl: In a patient older than 50, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, elevated inflammatory markers, and transient monocular visual loss strongly indicate giant cell arteritis.
objective: Recognize giant cell arteritis from the classic cranial ischemic and inflammatory presentation.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Anti-GBM autoantibodies target the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.
vignette: A 24-year-old man presents with hemoptysis, dyspnea, hematuria, and rapidly rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red-cell casts. Kidney biopsy demonstrates crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane.
distractors: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
IgA nephropathy
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
Microscopic polyangiitis
distractor_notes: GPA can cause pulmonary-renal disease but typically shows pauci-immune glomerulonephritis rather than linear anti-GBM IgG deposition and often has upper-airway disease.
IgA nephropathy produces mesangial IgA deposition and does not classically cause alveolar hemorrhage.
Poststreptococcal GN shows granular immune-complex deposition rather than linear IgG.
Microscopic polyangiitis is usually pauci-immune and ANCA-associated, not linear anti-GBM antibody disease.
key_expl: Goodpasture syndrome is anti-GBM disease involving both lungs and kidneys. Pulmonary hemorrhage plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with linear GBM IgG is diagnostic.
objective: Recognize Goodpasture syndrome from pulmonary hemorrhage, crescentic glomerulonephritis, and linear anti-GBM IgG deposition.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Phase I depolarizing neuromuscular block from succinylcholine
mechanism: Succinylcholine activates postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and maintains end-plate depolarization, inactivating nearby voltage-gated sodium channels and preventing generation of additional action potentials.
vignette: During rapid-sequence intubation, a patient receives succinylcholine. Brief fasciculations are followed by flaccid paralysis.
lead: Which mechanism best explains the initial neuromuscular blockade?
correct: Persistent motor-endplate depolarization with inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels
distractors: Competitive antagonism of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors without depolarization
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
Blockade of presynaptic calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal
Cleavage of SNARE proteins in cholinergic neurons
distractor_notes: Nondepolarizing blockers competitively antagonize nicotinic receptors without activating them.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition increases acetylcholine and is not the direct succinylcholine mechanism.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome involves presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release.
key_expl: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing nicotinic agonist. Sustained end-plate depolarization causes sodium-channel inactivation, so further action potentials cannot propagate until the membrane repolarizes.
objective: Explain phase I succinylcholine paralysis through persistent end-plate depolarization and sodium-channel inactivation.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Chronic acid reflux promotes metaplastic replacement of normal distal esophageal stratified squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with intestinal-type goblet cells, increasing adenocarcinoma risk.
vignette: A 56-year-old man with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease undergoes endoscopy. Biopsy of salmon-colored distal esophageal mucosa shows goblet cells.
correct: Replacement of stratified squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium
distractors: Replacement of columnar epithelium by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Dysplasia without a preceding change in epithelial cell type
Squamous metaplasia of gastric fundic epithelium
Replacement of esophageal epithelium by transitional urothelium
distractor_notes: Barrett esophagus proceeds from squamous toward columnar/intestinal-type epithelium, not the reverse.
Biopsy-proven goblet cells represent metaplasia; dysplasia may develop later but is not required for the initial adaptation.
Fundic gastric squamous metaplasia is not the lesion described.
Urothelium is not a physiologic metaplastic response in the esophagus.
key_expl: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus, with replacement of normal squamous mucosa by columnar epithelium containing goblet cells after chronic reflux injury.
objective: Recognize Barrett esophagus as intestinal-type columnar metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous epithelium.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary hemochromatosis from inappropriately low hepcidin activity
mechanism: Common HFE-associated hereditary hemochromatosis lowers hepcidin signaling, leaving ferroportin active on enterocytes and macrophages and increasing dietary iron absorption and iron release into plasma.
vignette: A 48-year-old man has diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy, elevated ferritin, and markedly increased transferrin saturation. Genetic testing identifies an HFE mutation.
lead: Which regulatory change most directly causes progressive iron loading?
correct: Decreased hepcidin activity with increased ferroportin-mediated iron export into plasma
distractors: Increased hepcidin activity causing ferroportin degradation
Reduced intestinal iron uptake due to suppressed ferroportin
Increased ferritin synthesis that prevents iron release from macrophages
Loss of transferrin receptors causing reduced systemic iron delivery
distractor_notes: High hepcidin lowers plasma iron; hereditary HFE hemochromatosis is characterized by insufficient hepcidin signaling.
Ferroportin remains active, increasing rather than reducing iron entry into plasma.
Ferritin is a storage protein and does not explain the primary regulatory defect.
Loss of transferrin receptors would impair iron utilization rather than cause classic systemic iron overload.
key_expl: Hepcidin normally binds ferroportin and promotes its internalization. Reduced hepcidin permits continued iron export from enterocytes and macrophages, producing excessive plasma iron and progressive tissue deposition.
objective: Explain HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis through reduced hepcidin and persistent ferroportin activity.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of cortisol feedback increases CRH and POMC-derived ACTH production; increased ACTH/MSH-related melanocortin signaling stimulates melanocytes and causes diffuse hyperpigmentation.
vignette: A patient with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency has fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and diffuse hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and oral mucosa.
lead: Which hormonal change most directly explains the skin findings?
correct: Increased ACTH and melanocortin signaling due to loss of cortisol negative feedback
distractors: Decreased ACTH secretion from the pituitary
Increased aldosterone stimulating melanocytes
Decreased proopiomelanocortin synthesis
Increased thyroid-stimulating hormone binding to melanocortin receptors
distractor_notes: Primary adrenal insufficiency raises ACTH because cortisol negative feedback is lost.
Aldosterone does not drive the characteristic hyperpigmentation.
POMC-derived ACTH/MSH signaling is increased rather than decreased.
TSH is not the primary mediator of Addison-related pigmentation.
key_expl: In primary adrenal failure, low cortisol removes negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Increased POMC/ACTH production increases melanocortin activity, leading to hyperpigmentation.
objective: Explain hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency through increased ACTH/POMC-derived melanocortin signaling.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Graves disease from stimulatory TSH-receptor antibodies
mechanism: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind and activate the TSH receptor, stimulating thyroid hormone synthesis and thyroid growth despite suppressed pituitary TSH.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, diffuse goiter, and exophthalmos. Free T4 is elevated and TSH is suppressed.
lead: Which immune mechanism most directly drives her thyroid hormone excess?
correct: Agonistic autoantibodies activating the TSH receptor
distractors: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes destroying thyroid follicular cells
Blocking autoantibodies preventing TSH-receptor activation
Immune-complex deposition in thyroid capillaries
Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase that directly inhibit hormone synthesis
distractor_notes: Destructive T-cell thyroiditis tends toward hypothyroidism rather than sustained Graves hyperthyroidism.
TSH-receptor blocking antibodies cause hypothyroid physiology.
Immune-complex deposition is not the central Graves mechanism.
Anti-TPO antibodies may coexist but do not directly produce Graves hyperthyroidism by stimulating hormone synthesis.
key_expl: Graves disease is driven by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that act as TSH-receptor agonists, causing diffuse thyroid growth and excess T3/T4 production.
objective: Identify stimulatory TSH-receptor autoantibodies as the mechanism of Graves hyperthyroidism.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia with splenic extravascular hemolysis
mechanism: Warm-reactive IgG coats RBCs at body temperature; splenic macrophages recognize Fc-coated cells, remove membrane, form spherocytes, and mediate predominantly extravascular hemolysis.
vignette: A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is low, reticulocyte count and indirect bilirubin are elevated, haptoglobin is low, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG. The smear shows spherocytes.
lead: Where does most red-cell destruction occur in this disorder?
correct: Splenic macrophages through Fc-mediated extravascular hemolysis
distractors: Renal glomeruli through immune-complex filtration
Bone marrow through complement-independent lysis of erythroblasts
Pulmonary capillaries through mechanical fragmentation
Liver only through direct IgM-mediated agglutination
distractor_notes: Warm AIHA destroys mature circulating RBCs primarily in the reticuloendothelial system, not through glomerular filtration.
Ineffective erythropoiesis is not the main mechanism of warm AIHA.
Mechanical fragmentation describes microangiopathic hemolysis.
Warm AIHA is primarily IgG mediated; IgM is characteristic of cold agglutinin disease.
key_expl: IgG-coated RBCs are recognized by Fc receptors on splenic macrophages. Partial phagocytosis creates microspherocytes and progressive splenic sequestration/destruction, making hemolysis predominantly extravascular.
objective: Explain warm AIHA as IgG-mediated splenic extravascular hemolysis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Benzodiazepine positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors
mechanism: Benzodiazepines bind an allosteric site on GABA-A receptors and, in the presence of GABA, increase the frequency of chloride-channel opening, enhancing postsynaptic hyperpolarization.
vignette: A patient with acute alcohol withdrawal is treated with diazepam and rapidly becomes less tremulous and agitated.
lead: Which change in ligand-gated ion-channel behavior mediates this drug class's effect?
correct: Increased frequency of GABA-A chloride-channel opening in the presence of GABA
distractors: Increased duration of GABA-A chloride-channel opening independent of drug class differences
Direct opening of GABA-A channels in the complete absence of GABA
Blockade of NMDA receptor channels by competitive antagonism at the glutamate site
Activation of GABA-B receptors to increase potassium conductance
distractor_notes: Barbiturates characteristically increase the duration of GABA-A channel opening; benzodiazepines increase frequency.
Benzodiazepines require GABA and act as positive allosteric modulators rather than direct channel openers at therapeutic concentrations.
NMDA antagonism is not the benzodiazepine mechanism.
GABA-B receptors are metabotropic and are activated by agents such as baclofen, not benzodiazepines.
key_expl: Benzodiazepines positively modulate GABA-A receptors by increasing the frequency of chloride-channel opening when GABA is bound, increasing chloride influx, neuronal hyperpolarization, and CNS inhibition.
objective: Distinguish benzodiazepine GABA-A modulation from barbiturate and GABA-B mechanisms.
